questions.q: Name the specific nephron segment where 100% of filtered glucose is normally reabsorbed, and identify the transport mechanism (including the co-transported ion) responsible.
questions.a: Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT); secondary active transport via SGLT2 (sodium-glucose linked transporter) co-transporting Na+ down its electrochemical gradient. A wrong answer (e.g., "DCT" or "facilitated diffusion alone") reveals the student confuses segment-specific transporter expression or misunderstands that glucose reabsorption is Na+-dependent, not passive.

questions.q: Explain why the descending limb of Henle's loop is permeable to water but the ascending limb is impermeable to water, and how this difference contributes to the medullary osmotic gradient.
questions.a: Descending limb expresses aquaporin-1 (constitutively water-permeable) allowing passive water efflux into hypertonic medulla, concentrating filtrate. Ascending limb lacks aquaporins but expresses NKCC2 (Na+-K+-2Cl- co-transporter) actively reabsorbing NaCl without water, diluting filtrate and depositing solute into interstitium. Wrong answers (e.g., "both limbs actively pump water") indicate confusion between passive osmotic water movement and active solute transport, or failure to link permeability differences to counter-current multiplication.

questions.q: A patient takes a loop diuretic (furosemide) that inhibits NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Predict the effect on: (a) medullary interstitial osmolarity, (b) urine volume, (c) urinary Ca2+ and Mg2+ excretion, and justify each.
questions.a: (a) Medullary osmolarity decreases because NaCl reabsorption into interstitium is blocked, collapsing the gradient. (b) Urine volume increases dramatically because without the gradient, collecting duct cannot reabsorb water even with ADH. (c) Ca2+/Mg2+ excretion increases because their paracellular reabsorption in thick ascending limb depends on the lumen-positive transepithelial voltage generated by NKCC2-mediated K+ recycling. Wrong predictions reveal inability to connect transporter inhibition to electrochemical consequences and downstream segment function.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the roles of PCT and collecting duct in HCO3- reabsorption and H+ secretion for acid-base balance. Include the key transporters and the fate of secreted H+ in each segment.
questions.a: PCT: Reabsorbs ~80-90% filtered HCO3- via apical NHE3 (Na+/H+ exchanger) secreting H+ that combines with luminal HCO3- to form H2CO3 → CO2 + H2O (catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase IV); CO2 diffuses into cell, reforms HCO3- via CA II, exits basolaterally via NBCe1. Collecting duct: Fine-tunes final urine pH via intercalated cells — type A (α-intercalated) secrete H+ via apical H+-ATPase and H+/K+-ATPase, reabsorb HCO3- basolaterally via AE1 (Cl-/HCO3- exchanger); type B secrete HCO3-. Secreted H+ in PCT is mostly "titrated" by filtered HCO3-; in collecting duct, H+ is buffered by NH3 (→ NH4+) and phosphate. Confusing the segments or transporters shows failure to grasp segmental specialization and the quantitative shift from bulk to regulatory reabsorption.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Aldosterone increases Na+ reabsorption in the collecting duct solely by inserting ENaC channels into the apical membrane." Identify what is correct, what is incomplete, and what additional mechanisms contribute.
questions.a: Partially correct but incomplete. Aldosterone (via mineralocorticoid receptor) does upregulate ENaC synthesis and apical insertion, but ALSO: (1) increases basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase density/activity to maintain low intracellular Na+, (2) upregulates ROMK (K+ channels) for K+ secretion to maintain electrical gradient, (3) enhances SGK1-mediated phosphorylation preventing ENaC retrieval, (4) acts on DCT (NCC) and CNT as well. Missing these reveals a reductionist view ignoring the coordinated basolateral-apical coupling and multi-segment action essential for net Na+ reabsorption and K+ excretion.

questions.q: Design a thought experiment using isolated perfused tubule microdissection to distinguish whether urea reabsorption in the inner medullary collecting duct (IMCD) is mediated by facilitated diffusion (UT-A1/UT-A3) versus passive paracellular leak. Specify the key measurements, controls, and expected outcomes for each hypothesis.
questions.a: Perfuse IMCD with radiolabeled urea ± phloretin (UT inhibitor) or high urea gradient; measure transepithelial urea flux (Jurea) and transepithelial voltage (Vt). Controls: (1) no urea gradient (equilibrium), (2) tight junction disruptor (EGTA) to test paracellular route. If facilitated: Jurea saturates at high [urea], inhibited by phloretin, Vt unchanged. If paracellular: Jurea linear with gradient, unaffected by phloretin, abolished by EGTA. Poor design (e.g., no voltage measurement, no saturation test) reveals inability to apply kinetic and pharmacological criteria to distinguish transporter-mediated vs. passive paracellular transport.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Tubular ______ is the selective process by which the renal tubules reclaim essential substances (water, glucose, amino acids, ions) from the glomerular filtrate back into the peritubular capillaries, while tubular secretion is the active transport of specific waste products (H+, K+, NH3, drugs, toxins) from peritubular capillaries into the tubular lumen for excretion, together converting 180 L/day of filtrate into ~1.5 L/day of concentrated urine.

Fill in the blank: Imagine drinking 2 litres of nimbu pani on a hot Delhi afternoon — your kidneys must reclaim that water and the precious glucose, sodium, and ______ from 180 litres of daily filtrate while dumping excess H+ and K+ into urine.
What is Tubular reabsorption? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Tubular reabsorption is the selective process by which the renal tubules reclaim essential substances (water, glucose, amino acids, ions) from the glomerular filtrate back into the peritubular capillaries, while tubular secretion is the active transport of specific waste products (H+, K+, NH3, drugs, toxins) from peritubular capillaries.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Tubular reabsorption?
questions.a: Students believe "water follows salt passively everywhere in the nephron" and fail to recognize that water permeability is segment-specific and hormonally regulated — e.g., they think ascending limb reabsorbs water because it reabsorbs NaCl, or that collecting duct is always water-permeable.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can trace the fate of Na+, glucose, water, urea, H+, and K+ through each nephron segment (PCT, Henle's loop, DCT, collecting duct), identify the transport mechanism (active/passive, transcellular/paracellular) and hormonal regulation at each step, and explain how reabsorption and secretion jointly maintain blood pH, osmolarity.
